about.p1: jasScience is a next-generation ecosystem built to unify complex mathematical computation, molecular modeling, and real-time interactive visualization. We build the bridge between high-load backend systems and fluid web interfaces.
about.p2: Our platform lets researchers, engineers, and students design physical and chemical experiments with minimal latency. Machine-learning algorithms predict the behavior of dynamic systems before heavy server-side computation even runs.
about.d2024: First 2D particle-simulation algorithms and optimized C# .NET computation kernels.
about.d2025: Interactive graphics engine and neural assistants for live scientific data analysis.
about.d2026: A full platform with distributed computation and team collaboration support.
about.bio1: Leads the team and builds the Java backend and distributed computation services.
about.bio2: Designs the product interface and develops research workflows across the web stack.
about.bio3: Builds machine-learning algorithms, physics models, and reliable backend services.
about.teamDesc: Our team is made up of engineers obsessed with high performance, clean code, and user comfort. Every module is strictly optimized to sustain 60 FPS even under millions of data points.
about.copilotMsg1: "The team is assembled! Ready to launch the laboratory on your signal."

cover.subtitle2: An Interactive Guide to Experimental Chemistry

contents.p1: This journal is not just a collection of facts. It is a researcher's working tool. Recorded here are observations, mistakes, and experiments we conducted at jasScience.
contents.p2: Every instrument, reaction, and formula you'll find on these pages is intrinsically linked to the Sandbox. The book and the simulation are one. Study theory here, then test hypotheses in practice.
contents.p3: Remember: an experiment begins not with a reaction, but with observation.

intro.title: Introduction
intro.p1: Chemistry is not magic, though it often looks like it. It is a rigorous science of transformations, requiring precision, patience, and respect for nature's laws.
intro.p2: In this guide, we have gathered the basic principles of working in a modern virtual laboratory. There are no superfluous words—only what will help you conduct a successful experiment. We will start with basic concepts and gradually move to complex setups.
intro.p3: Every researcher must know their equipment. It is important to understand why an Erlenmeyer flask has its specific shape and how to properly connect a Liebig condenser.
intro.fig1: Fig. 01 — An experiment begins not with a reaction, but with observation.
intro.p4: Starting from this page, I will try to record everything that happens in the laboratory. Not for beauty — for accuracy. A good experiment begins before the burner is lit.
intro.p5: One of the first lessons of the laboratory: the difference between what you expected to see and what actually happened — that is the starting point of science.

lavoisier.name: Antoine Lavoisier
lavoisier.p1: The father of modern chemistry. He transformed alchemical speculations into an exact science based on strict measurements.
lavoisier.p2: Before Lavoisier, scientists believed in 'phlogiston'—a mythical substance released during combustion. Lavoisier proved that combustion is a process of combining with oxygen.
lavoisier.quote: "Nothing is created, either in the operations of art or in those of nature, and it may be considered as a general principle that in every operation there exists an equal quantity of matter before and after the operation."
lavoisier.p3: In our Sandbox, the mass of a closed system always remains constant, regardless of the reactions occurring inside the flask.

mendeleev.name: Dmitri Mendeleev
mendeleev.p1: The scientist who saw order in chaos. He arranged elements by atomic mass and discovered a fundamental law of nature, predicting properties of undiscovered elements.
mendeleev.p2: The periodic table is not just a catalog; it's a map of the chemical universe. In our laboratory, the properties of every substance stem from the very laws he structured.
mendeleev.quote: "Science begins when you begin to measure. Exact science is inconceivable without measure."
mendeleev.p3: The simulator features a built-in element atlas, allowing you to predict how unknown reagents will behave.

curie.name: Marie Curie
curie.p1: A pioneer in radioactivity research, the only woman to be awarded a Nobel Prize twice.
curie.p2: Her work showed that the atom is not indivisible—it contains immense internal energy. The discovery of radium and polonium revolutionized our understanding of matter.
curie.quote: "Nothing in life is to be feared, it is only to be understood. Now is the time to understand more, so that we may fear less."
curie.p3: In the laboratory, we carefully simulate energy balances and safety protocols when working with high-energy reactions.

boyle.name: Robert Boyle
boyle.p1: One of the founders of modern chemistry, who first applied the strict experimental method. He proved that gas volume is inversely proportional to pressure.
boyle.p2: Boyle's law is the first step in understanding gas behavior. It forms the basis of steam condensers and closed systems.
boyle.quote: "He that investigates nature should first of all accustom himself to doubt."
boyle.p3: You will witness this law in action when you heat liquid in a closed flask, watching the vapor pressure rise.

sandbox.subtitle: Where theory becomes action
sandbox.p1: The virtual laboratory provides complete freedom. It is not a set of scripted animations, but a physically accurate simulation of temperature, pressure, phase transitions, and reactions.
sandbox.p2: You can assemble any setup: from simply heating water in a beaker to a complex distillation system with a reflux condenser.
sandbox.caption_diagram: Fig. 3.1 — Three working modes of the Sandbox.
sandbox.p3: Every object on the workspace has ports — connection points. Liquid ports transfer substances, thermal ports transfer energy, gas ports work with vapor and pressure. Correct port connection is the foundation of a working setup.
sandbox.p4: Inspector — the right panel showing the properties of the selected object. Here you can see the current temperature, liquid level, pressure and state. Inspector allows fine-tuning of parameters before running the simulation.

equipment.title: APPARATUS CATALOG
equipment.p1: Instruments are an extension of the chemist's hands. It is important to know the purpose of each vessel and its physical limits.

detail.title: TECHNICAL DATA
detail.fig: Fig. 14 — Borosilicate glass, withstands up to 500°C.
detail.purpose: The conical shape prevents splashing when mixing liquids and allows for easy corking. Ideal for titration.
detail.portIn: Top opening accepts liquids (e.g., from a burette).
detail.portVapor: Open for gas evaporation unless sealed with a stopper.
detail.portHeat: Flat base is optimal for placement on a hot plate.

scenario.title: INDEX
scenario.p1: This section contains step-by-step instructions for conducting basic and advanced experiments.
scenario.p2: Each scenario is prepared so that you can load it directly into the Sandbox. The setup will assemble automatically; you just monitor the temperature, add reagents, and draw conclusions.

physics.title: HEAT TRANSFER
physics.name: Engine Physics
physics.p1: The laboratory operates on a thermodynamic model. Every flask, hot plate, and drop of liquid continuously exchanges energy.
physics.p2: Understand that the plate doesn't heat water instantly. Heat transfers from the coil to the glass, and from glass to liquid. This gradient can lead to thermal shock.

safety.title: RULES
safety.p1: In the simulator, a flask can explode. Glass shatters from thermal stress, and closed systems burst from excessive pressure.
safety.p2: Follow these rules to ensure your experiments complete without triggering the emergency shutdown system.
safety.rule1: Do not place a cold flask on a scorching hot plate. Heat gradually.
safety.rule2: When heating gases, ensure an open port (Vapor) or attach an expansion vessel.
safety.rule3: Keep the Bunsen burner away from highly flammable substances like ethanol.

conclusion.p1: We have come a long way from the basic laws of mass conservation to assembling complex systems.
conclusion.p2: But chemistry is not just a set of completed experiments. It is an ongoing process of questioning nature. Your Sandbox now awaits your own hypotheses.
conclusion.quote: The book ends. The experiment does not.

chemistry.p1: Chemistry is the science of substances and their transformations. It studies the composition, structure and properties of matter, as well as the conditions under which some substances transform into others. Every object around us is the result of chemical processes that have been ongoing for billions of years.
chemistry.p2: Unlike physics, which describes the physical properties of matter without changing its composition, chemistry studies transformations: how atoms rearrange themselves, forming new molecules with completely different properties. Rust on iron, burning wood, cooking food — these are all chemical reactions.
chemistry.p3: The subject of chemistry spans the entire range: from the simplest elements in the periodic table to the most complex DNA molecules. That is why chemistry is connected to biology, physics, geology, medicine and technology.
chemistry.box1_1: Chemistry — study of composition and transformations of matter
chemistry.box1_2: Substance — what all bodies consist of
chemistry.box1_3: Phenomenon — any change occurring with a substance
chemistry.box1_4: Chemical reaction — process of transforming some substances into others
chemistry.box2_content: Chemistry studies only those changes in which new substances are formed. Physical changes (melting ice, water evaporation) are not considered chemical.
chemistry.caption1: Fig. 1.1 — Law of conservation of mass: the mass of reactants equals the mass of products.
chemistry.caption2: Fig. 1.2 — States of matter: solid, liquid, gas.

history.intro: For thousands of years, humanity observed chemical phenomena without understanding their nature. The path from alchemy to modern science took more than two thousand years and required revolutionary discoveries that shattered previous notions of matter.
history.period1_text: Egyptians, Greeks and Chinese discovered metallurgy, glassmaking and dyeing. The first 'chemists' were craftsmen who worked with fire and metals.
history.period2_text: Arab and European alchemists sought the philosopher's stone and the elixir of immortality. Despite their mysticism, they developed important laboratory methods: distillation, crystallization, sublimation.
history.period3_text: Boyle rejected alchemical elements and introduced the concept of 'chemical element'. Lavoisier discovered the law of conservation of mass and systematized nomenclature.
history.period4_text: Dalton proposed atomic theory. Mendeleev created the periodic table. Curie discovered radioactivity. This was an era of great systematizations.
history.period5_text: Quantum mechanics explained chemical bonding. Polymers, pharmaceuticals, nanochemistry and computational chemistry changed the world. Today, chemistry is inseparable from biology and physics.

jabir.p1: The Arab scholar Jabir ibn Hayyan, known in Europe as Geber, is considered the father of chemistry. He was the first to systematically describe laboratory processes: distillation, calcination, evaporation and crystallization. His works were translated into Latin and formed the basis of European alchemy.
jabir.p2: The Persian scholar al-Razi classified chemical substances into animal, plant and mineral categories — the first systematic classification. He also described sulfuric acid and developed methods for its production. His 'Book of Secrets' contains detailed instructions on chemical operations.

practice.p01_question: Which instrument must be connected to the hot plate to monitor the liquid temperature?
practice.p01_goal: Goal: assemble a heating system with temperature control.
practice.p01_feedback_correct: Correct. The thermometer has a thermal port that allows reading the liquid temperature in real time.
practice.p01_feedback_wrong: Not quite. This instrument does not have a port for measuring liquid temperature.
practice.p02_question: Which equipment is used for precise measurement and drop-by-drop liquid delivery?
practice.p02_feedback_correct: Correct. The burette is a precision titration instrument with a graduated scale and stopcock for delivery control.
practice.p02_feedback_wrong: Not quite. Try again — think about precision dosing.
practice.p03_question: Which substance has the formula H₂O and is the main solvent in most chemical reactions?
practice.p03_feedback_correct: Correct. H₂O is water. A polar solvent, universal for most reactions in living and non-living nature.
practice.p03_feedback_wrong: Incorrect. Recall the composition of the water molecule: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
practice.p04_question: In what order should you assemble the setup for heating a liquid with temperature measurement?
practice.p04_step2: Place the beaker on the plate
practice.p04_feedback: Correct sequence! This is the recommended order for assembling any laboratory setup: first the base, then the vessels, then sensors and connections.
